linux.fallback: rpm/dnf .repo files under /etc/yum.repos.d are not read yet (a host whose /etc/yum.repos.d has entries reports constrained linux:rpm_repo:planned); zypper, pacman and apk sources are not read, so zero rows there is not evidence of none

macos.fallback: not read yet: one unsupported status row, macos:planned

windows.fallback: not read yet: one unsupported status row, windows:planned

caveats: **No documented customer driver.** The capability map's "Patch Connectivity Testing" row checks that update sources are reachable, not whether they are trustworthy, and the SOC 2 supply-chain material covers Yuzu's own build pipeline rather than a customer endpoint's package sources. The plugin exists on capability-gap reasoning alone.

**Facts only.** The plugin is read-only and reports how sources are configured; an unsigned or unexpected source is a row, not a verdict. It does not enforce, fetch, verify a signature or resolve a key, and enforcement posture belongs to the sibling posture plugins.

**rpm/dnf family planned.** The yum/dnf `.repo` settings (`gpgcheck`, `repo_gpgcheck`, `gpgkey`, `sslverify`) are not read. A Linux host whose `/etc/yum.repos.d` has entries reports `CONSTRAINED` with `linux:rpm_repo:planned` and no `rpm_repo` rows, so it never reads as having no sources; a host without that directory (Debian, Ubuntu) stays `supported`.

**macOS and Windows legs planned.** The macOS Software Update policy (local and MDM-managed `com.apple.SoftwareUpdate.plist`) and the Windows WSUS and Automatic Updates policy (`HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate`) are not read; each leg reports one `unsupported` status row.

**Known limits of the apt read.** A `Signed-By` key is reported by path or fingerprint text, not resolved, and `/usr/share/keyrings` is not inventoried; global apt configuration (`apt.conf`, `apt.conf.d`) is not read, so `unset` never means "enforced". Only the apt family is modelled, so zypper, pacman and apk hosts report zero rows and `supported`, and options other than `signed-by`, `trusted`, `enabled` and `allow-insecure` are ignored; a file a writer keeps empty for the whole read looks genuinely empty.

definitions.description: Reports how the device's package and update sources are configured to trust their signing authorities, as facts only. On Linux, one row per apt source (one-line and deb822, with signed-by, trusted and, for one-line entries only, allow-insecure) and one row per apt keyring file. The yum/dnf repository family is planned and not yet read; a Linux host whose /etc/yum.repos.d has entries reports a constrained status with linux:rpm_repo:planned instead of rows. The macOS Software Update and Windows WSUS legs are planned and not yet read. Only the apt family is read: on a Linux host whose sources live elsewhere (zypper, pacman, apk) zero rows is not evidence that no sources exist. Global apt configuration (apt.conf, apt.conf.d) is not read, so an unset trust field is not evidence that signatures are enforced. A leading status row states whether the read was complete. The plugin never enforces, fetches or changes anything.

description: Package and update-source trust posture (facts only)
how_it_works:
`sources` reports facts about how the device's package and update sources are configured to trust their signing authorities. It reads local configuration files and nothing else: no subprocess, no network fetch, no write. The first row is always a `status` row saying whether the read was complete; the data rows follow, one per source line or stanza and one per keyring file. It reports what is configured and leaves any judgement, and any enforcement, to the consumer and to the sibling posture plugins.

On Linux the plugin reads the apt family. Source files come from `/etc/apt/sources.list` and `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/` in both the one-line and the deb822 format, and each row carries the `signed-by`, `trusted`, `enabled` and (one-line only) `allow-insecure` settings. The keyrings in `/etc/apt/trusted.gpg`, `/etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/` and `/etc/apt/keyrings/` are listed with their format and size; key material is never emitted. The plugin also lists `/etc/yum.repos.d` by name without opening any `.repo` file, and when that directory has entries the result is `CONSTRAINED` with `linux:rpm_repo:planned`, so an rpm host never reads as having no sources. On macOS and Windows the plugin reads nothing and answers with one `unsupported` status row (`macos:planned` or `windows:planned`).

Reads are bounded and conservative. A symlink as the final component of a file or directory is refused, never followed. A source file over 1 MiB, a directory over 1,024 entries, rows beyond a 1 MiB total, or more than 16 MiB read in one run stops that part of the walk and is reported, never silently truncated. In `sources.list.d` only the files apt itself reads are reported (not hidden, names within `[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]`, suffix `.list` or `.sources`). Keyrings are chosen by suffix alone (`*.gpg` and `*.asc` in `trusted.gpg.d`, any name in `/etc/apt/keyrings`), because apt before 3.0 trusts a key under any such name; apt 3.0 and later skip odd names there, so an extra row can appear on those hosts. An entry apt itself would refuse is counted as `unparsed_entry` and produces no row. A NUL or non-UTF-8 byte in a reported field is replaced with `?` and flagged `invalid_bytes`. A file whose size or modification time changes while it is read, or that is empty and was modified within the last two seconds, is flagged `modified_during_read` instead of being reported as read.

### What you can decide with it

Each data row is one fact an operator can act on. On Linux (apt hosts):

| Question | Where to look | Reading it |
|---|---|---|
| Is signature checking switched off for a source? | `apt_source` fields 8 and 9 (`trusted`, `allow_insecure`) | `yes` means apt skips signature checking for that source. `unset` means the source does not say; it does not prove checking is enforced, because global apt settings are not read. |
| Does a source pin its own key, or rely on every globally trusted key? | `apt_source` field 7 (`signed_by`) | A path or fingerprint pins the source to that key. `-` means apt falls back to its global trusted keyrings. `inline_key` means the key is embedded in the file. |
| Which keys does apt trust for every source? | `apt_keyring` rows with scope `legacy_trusted_gpg` or `trusted_gpg_d` | Every key in those files is a global trust anchor. Rows in scope `etc_apt_keyrings` are only trusted where a `signed-by` names them. |
| Where does this host install software from? | `apt_source` URIs, suites, components | The URI list, with any `user:pass@` redacted. A disabled source shows `enabled` = `no`. |

What it cannot tell you: who owns a keyring file or whether its key is valid (no fingerprint is computed), whether a URI is reachable or legitimate, anything about rpm/dnf, zypper, pacman or apk hosts, or the macOS and Windows update policy. A clean result (`OK`, zero or more rows, no `trusted=yes`) proves only that the apt source files that were read do not disable verification; it does not prove an apt host is hardened, and zero rows on a non-apt host says nothing. There is no workflow to follow: the action is read-only and takes no parameters.

### Diagrams

The diagram follows one candidate file through the Linux read. A file that is merely absent is not a failure, while every other way of not reading it completely becomes a token that turns the whole result into `CONSTRAINED`, so a source that could not be read is never reported as absent or unsigned. Rows that were read are still returned alongside the tokens.
name: update_source_trust

columns.description: Row shape discriminator (field 0). Values: status, apt_source, apt_keyring.
columns.name: row_kind

columns.description: status: the literal "sources". apt_source: the logical absolute path of the source file. apt_keyring: the keyring file path.
columns.name: field_1

columns.description: status: supported, constrained or unsupported (Windows and macOS, whose legs read nothing, and a leg that threw report unsupported). apt_source: format, one_line or deb822. apt_keyring: scope (legacy_trusted_gpg, trusted_gpg_d or etc_apt_keyrings).
columns.name: field_2

columns.description: status: reason token(s) for a constrained or unsupported read, "-" when complete; a token has the form <os>:<source>:<detail> (linux:rpm_repo:planned on a Linux host whose /etc/yum.repos.d has entries) or <os>:<state> (windows:planned on Windows, macos:planned on macOS). apt_source: source types, space-separated when several (deb, deb-src or unmodelled). apt_keyring: key format (armored, binary, empty or unmodelled).
columns.name: field_3

columns.description: apt_source: URIs (space-separated when the entry lists several), userinfo (user:pass@) redacted. apt_keyring: size in bytes. Not used by status.
columns.name: field_4

columns.description: apt_source: signed_by, the Signed-By value (paths and/or fingerprints), the literal inline_key when a deb822 Signed-By embeds a key block (key material is never emitted), the literal unmodelled when a one-line signed-by uses += or -=, or "-" when absent (apt then uses its global trusted keyrings).
columns.name: field_7

columns.description: apt_source: trusted (yes, no, unset, unmodelled; yes disables signature checking for the source; only the apt boolean words are recognised and any other value is unmodelled; unset means the source does not say, not that signatures are enforced).
columns.name: field_8

columns.description: apt_source: allow_insecure (yes, no, unset, unmodelled; read from the one-line [allow-insecure=...] option only: apt ignores it in deb822, so it is unset there).
columns.name: field_9

columns.description: apt_source: enabled (yes, no, unmodelled; deb822 defaults to enabled).
columns.name: field_10

outputs_note: Every row is pipe-delimited; field 0 is the row kind and the first row is always `status|sources|<supported\|constrained\|unsupported>|<reason or ->`. The kinds are `apt_source` and `apt_keyring`; the rpm/dnf, macOS and Windows legs emit no data rows (caveats 3 and 4). Every row of a kind has the same field count, and `-` is an absent value. Booleans use one four-value vocabulary: `yes`, `no`, `unset` (the key is absent) and `unmodelled` (the key is present with a value the plugin does not recognise). A host that has no apt configuration reports zero rows and stays `supported`: an absent thing is not a failure (the deferred rpm/dnf family is the exception, see Result status). Free text is escaped for the server's pipe grammar (`safe_output_field`, lossy on backslash by design) and URL userinfo (`user:pass@`) is redacted. `update_source_trust` is not in the server's key/value plugin set, so rows are decoded as pipe-separated fields, not as `key|rest`. The columns below are the widest shapes; narrower shapes use a prefix of them. The `Available` column lists the OSes whose leg emits that field; macOS and Windows read nothing today, so only the status row's fields (`row_kind` to `field_3`) are populated there (caveat 4). A deb822 stanza that lists several types, URIs, suites or components is one row with the values space-separated (`bookworm bookworm-updates`), and each keyring file is its own row.

privileges.if_refused: `CONSTRAINED` / partial with a `linux:apt_sources:<detail>` or `linux:apt_keyring:<detail>` token (or `linux:rpm_repo:<detail>` when the `/etc/yum.repos.d` listing itself is refused); the unreadable source is absent from the rows, never reported as unsigned or absent
privileges.measured: Not measured on the `yuzu-agent` account: the only capture (`docs/samples/linux.txt`) ran as root in a container, which bypasses permission bits, so it proves the read path and the row shapes, not the grant
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, dedicated unprivileged account (`yuzu-agent` on the packaged unit), never root by design (`docs/agent-privilege-model.md`)

result_status.when: Linux: every read completed, populated or genuinely empty (no `/etc/yum.repos.d` entries). On a host whose sources live outside apt and rpm/dnf (zypper, pacman, apk) zero rows is NOT evidence of no sources (caveat 5)

a source exists but could not be read completely or decoded; the rows that were read are still emitted. `permission_denied`: the agent account cannot read the path. `symlink_refused` / `not_a_directory`: a final path component is a symbolic link (never followed) or a file sits where a directory belongs. `not_regular`: a FIFO, socket, device or directory sits where a file belongs. `oversized` / `entry_cap` / `output_cap`: a file over 1 MiB, a directory over 1,024 entries, or rows past the 1 MiB total budget (the rest was not read). `input_cap`: the walk pulled more than 16 MiB of source and keyring bytes from the kernel, counting failed reads; the rest was not read. `short_read` / `modified_during_read`: the file changed while it was read. `invalid_bytes`: a NUL or non-UTF-8 byte in a reported field after redaction was replaced with `?`. `unparsed_entry`: an entry apt itself would refuse. `open_failed` / `read_failed` / `dir_open_failed` / `io_error` / `enumeration_error`: an operating-system operation failed
`/etc/yum.repos.d` has entries and the rpm/dnf `.repo` family is not read (caveat 3); the apt rows that were read are still emitted

result_status.provenance: `windows:leg:exception:<category>` / `linux:leg:exception:<category>` / `macos:leg:exception:<category>`, `<category>` one of `bad_alloc`, `std_exception`, `unknown` (the exception text is deliberately never carried)
result_status.when: a leg threw: one `status|sources|unsupported|<os>:leg:exception:<category>` row, reported instead of unwinding across the plugin boundary. Under sustained allocation failure the category suffix can be lost, leaving the bare `<os>:leg:exception`, and the row itself may not be written; the typed status (or a non-zero rc) still reaches the host. A leg that throws after it has already reported (an allocation failure while its rows are being written) leaves this `unsupported` row BEHIND the rows already written, after the leading `supported` or `constrained` row: the one case with two `status` rows, where the first is not the outcome; the last `status` row and the typed status are the outcome.

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`. `sources` is also a gathered definition (`crossplatform.security.update_source_trust`, 300s TTL).
**Not consumed by** daily-sync, TAR, DEX, or metrics.

**Sensitivity.** Rows name the repositories a device installs software from (URIs, key paths), which discloses part of its software supply chain. URL userinfo (`user:pass@`) is redacted in every URL-bearing field; a secret carried in a URL query string or path (a vendor entitlement token) cannot be recognised and is emitted as written, and so is any user name inside a configured path or URL (`file:///home/<user>/repo`, `signed-by=/home/<user>/key.gpg`, `~user`): the plugin adds none of its own. Key material is never emitted, only key file paths, formats and sizes. Rows stay in the ResponseStore for the response retention period (90 days by default) and are not purged individually, so treat a credential seen in a row as exposed and rotate it.
**Siblings:** `windows_updates` (patch compliance and reachability of update sources, not their trust) and `installed_apps` (what is installed, not where it came from).
